name: Nandi
role: Sacred bull, gatekeeper and mount of Shiva
summary: Nandi is the patient white bull who sits facing Shiva in almost every Shiva temple. Devotees whisper wishes to him, and tradition also honours him as a teacher and a doorkeeper.
about: In Shaiva tradition Nandi is Shiva's devoted bull and chief attendant. Some old texts use the name for a doorkeeper rather than a bull, and Siddhanta writings still keep Nandi and the bull Vrishabha apart. The Shiva Purana says he arose from a sacrifice held by the sage Shilada, who had prayed hard for a child. Tradition says he later practised penance on the Narmada river to earn the role of gatekeeper and mount. Shaiva Agamas give the rules for placing him in a temple: seated on the central axis, facing the linga. Siddhanta texts name him as the first of the Siddhars, who passed on Shiva's teaching to eight disciples. Some sources describe him as a human-bodied figure with a bull's head, while temples mostly show a calm seated bull.
kidSummary: Nandi is a big, gentle bull who sits outside Shiva's shrine and keeps watch. He looks at Shiva with so much love that he never turns away. Many children are told that if you whisper a wish in his ear, he carries it to Shiva.

story.title: A wished-for child
story.text: The sage Shilada wanted a child. According to the Shiva Purana, after long prayer, Nandi arose from the sacrifice he performed, and Shilada raised him as his son.

story.title: A bright young learner
story.text: Nandi grew up wise and devoted to Shiva. Traditions say he did penance on the banks of the Narmada, hoping to serve Shiva closely.

story.title: The gatekeeper
story.text: Shiva was pleased and made Nandi his gatekeeper and his mount. Nandi sat at the door of Kailasa and watched over everyone who came.

story.title: Teacher of sages
story.text: In Siddhanta texts, Nandi learned deep teachings from Shiva and Parvati. He is said to have passed them on to eight disciples, who went to eight directions to share them.

story.title: A wish whispered
story.text: In temples today, a stone Nandi sits facing the shrine. Many devotees quietly whisper their wishes into his ear, hoping he will carry them to Shiva.

teaches: Keeping your attention on what matters
places: Yaganti Uma Maheswara Temple, Andhra Pradesh

facts.text: In the oldest texts the name Nandi belongs to a doorkeeper of Shiva, not to the bull, and Siddhanta writings still tell the two apart.
A temple Nandi sits facing the inner shrine and stands for the soul, always keeping its attention on Shiva. In the yogic reading he is the mind given to Shiva, the guru within.
In one Puranic legend, Nandi cursed Ravana's Lanka to be burned by a monkey, because Ravana fidgeted like one while waiting to meet Shiva. Hanuman later set Lanka ablaze.
The Tiruvilaiyadal Puranam tells that Nandi took the form of a whale to bring Shiva and Parvati together; Parvati became a fisherwoman and Shiva a fisherman who caught the whale.
Nandi images are not found only in India. The seated bull turns up in Shiva temples in Southeast Asia too, including Cambodia, and the Nandi page lists one at Prambanan in Java.
Many devotees whisper their wishes into Nandi's right ear, believing he will relay them to Shiva.
On the 700th step up Chamundi Hills in Mysuru, a huge granite Nandi sits in front of a small Shiva temple. Mysore's Maharaja Dodda Devaraja Wodeyar had it set up in 1664.
Thanjavur's single-stone Nandi is given as about 3.7 m high, 6 m long and 2.6 m wide in a 1975 survey, and weighs roughly 25 tonnes.
Atop the 80-tonne granite block that crowns the Brihadisvara tower, pairs of Nandi figures sit at the corners, each roughly 2 m across.
At the Yaganti temple in Andhra Pradesh, devotees believe the stone Nandi keeps growing. Locals say it was once much smaller, and a pillar had to be removed to make room for it.
A prophecy credited to the saint Veerabrahmendra Swami says the stone Nandi of Yaganti will come alive and call out when the Kali Yuga ends.
At Yaganti, fresh water from the hillside flows into the temple pond through the mouth of a stone Nandi, and locals say no one knows how the pond stays full all year.
Near the Veerabhadra Temple in Lepakshi sits a granite Nandi carved from one block, about 6 m high and 9 m long, said to be among the largest of its kind in the world.
Bengaluru's Bull Temple was built in 1537 under Kempe Gowda. Its Nandi is about 4.6 m high and 6.1 m long, and the stone is kept covered with fresh layers of butter.
The name Nandikeshvara is also borne by an ancient theatre scholar credited with the Abhinaya Darpana, or Mirror of Gesture. Historians place his school between the 5th and 2nd centuries BCE.
On Pradosha, the twilight fast to Shiva held on the thirteenth day of each fortnight, Nandi is worshipped in Shiva temples and Shiva and Parvati are carried in procession seated on him.
At Thanjavur's Brihadisvara Temple, Nandi has a pillared hall of his own in front of the main shrine, and its ceiling carries old Nayaka-era murals.
Regional legend places Nandi's penance on the Narmada at Tripur Tirth, which is now the Nandikeshwar Temple in Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh.
Nandi, shown as a seated bull, was the emblem of Tamil Shaiva rulers such as the Pallavas and the Jaffna kings. Today it is the flag of Shaivism, first raised in Sri Lanka in 1998.
Kannada speakers call the sacred bull Basava, which is why Bengaluru's famous Nandi temple and its neighbourhood are known as Basavanagudi.
